commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[zephyr] Add opt-in intra-shard map execution (#9995)

Add `ZephyrContext(intra_shard_execution=IntraShardExecution.AUTO)` to
execute row maps, filters, selections, and flat maps within an existing
shard across workers. Callbacks must not depend on per-shard mutable
state. The default is `OFF`. The planner adds `Split → Map → Concat`
when Parquet source fragments can feed idle workers or a later reshard
leaves fewer shards than workers. It reads footer row counts and aims
for four source tasks per worker, capped at one task per row. There is
no byte minimum because row callbacks can be expensive inference calls.
Existing source shards that fill the worker pool keep fused row
execution. Maps following `group_by` stay on whole output shards.
Ordered concatenation restores original shard IDs, row order, and output
filenames before shard-level operations and writes.

Maps immediately preceding an explicit-schema Parquet sink produce
Parquet fragments for an Arrow-batch final writer. Other map
intermediates use pickle chunks. Concatenation avoids a key shuffle, but
final assembly still decodes and re-encodes Parquet. Batch-mode sources
retain their batch boundaries, and `map_shard` callbacks remain
indivisible.

Fixed local samples from TaskTrove dataset revision
`02923004846e4e73862c20962f823a6d05100e7a`, each with one row group,
used [conversion code at
ee20e03517](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ee20e03517/experiments/post_training/task_curation)
through Zephyr's `SubprocessRunner`. All columns use `AUTO`; one worker
retains fused execution. Single-run wall times on a shared Ryzen 7 3800X
include startup, intermediate I/O, final write, and shutdown:

| Sample | Rows | 1 worker | 2 workers | 4 workers |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Structured outputs | 10,000 | 79.81s | 58.77s | 34.93s |
| SWE-smith | 2,000 | 33.93s | 31.09s | 21.83s |
| SWE-rebench | 2,000 | 19.90s | 23.33s | 20.37s |
| TACO | 2,000 | 68.80s | 36.74s | 24.44s |

All runs matched the one-worker baseline's complete record content,
rejection outcomes, source order, and single output file layout.
Four-worker final Parquet read/write took 3.47–9.75s; SWE-rebench showed
no end-to-end improvement. Peak summed process-tree RSS ranged from 2.25
to 3.00 GiB at four workers. Workers still read overlapping row groups
in full, so row offsets increase read work and memory. Host load varied
during these runs; they are not stable throughput estimates. These runs
used the earlier source task sizing; the four-task target has not been
benchmarked. The sizing design and edge cases are recorded in the
[design artifact](https://loom.oa.dev/s/68n20qo1/artifacts/design).

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[haliax] Add Pallas-Triton tile-map ragged_dot kernels for AMD GPUs (#10009)

On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now
runs a second family of Pallas-Triton grouped-GEMM kernels, called
tile-map kernels. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as
before. NVIDIA keeps the existing group-grid kernels and block sizes,
including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. Those kernels are unchanged in
the diff. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the
tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a
follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

These kernels use Pallas-Triton, which JAX 0.11 deprecates; Mosaic GPU,
the replacement JAX suggests, does not support ROCm. #9859 ports the
same kernels to Triton launched through `jax_triton.triton_call`, but
jax-triton kernels hang multi-GPU training on ROCm today. On a kernel's
first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary
file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so when the 8 GPUs
of one process launch together, all but one fail and the step stalls at
the next collective (evidence in #9859). This PR lands the Pallas-Triton
version so AMD runs can use the tile-map kernels now. #9859 replaces
them once a jaxlib release fixes the race.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and
exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and
input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile,
column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in
megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in
place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat
grid over all groups. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The
old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family
table that was swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new:
chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows
(`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is
TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 453824). The June
expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 94 → 594 | 88 → 635 | 378 → 483 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 587 → 730 | 556 → 808 | 428 → 585 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 525 → 735 | 511 → 818 | 429 → 579 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 560 → 668 | 541 → 765 | 403 → 586 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 425 → 771 | 383 → 861 | 435
→ 593 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 629 → 792 | 596 → 898 | 449 → 591 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s
on this GPU. A sweep of `group_m` from 1 to 16 and `num_xcds` of 1 or 8
ran at both shape sets. Every setting beat the old kernels, and the
chosen AMD entries are within 5% of the best setting sampled.

The full June model ran on 8x MI350X with EP8, `gpu_pallas_triton_flash`
attention, memory fraction 0.90 and 20 steps. The table gives the median
step over steps 2-19:

| Remat | Batch | Old kernels | New kernels | Peak memory (new) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| recompute_all | 64 | 2.149 s (122.0k tok/s) | 1.853 s (141.5k tok/s) |
158.4 GiB |
| recompute_all | 96 | 3.080 s (127.7k tok/s) | 2.696 s (145.9k tok/s) |
164.7 GiB |
| save_moe | 64 | 1.988 s (131.9k tok/s) | 1.832 s (143.1k tok/s) |
205.8 GiB |
| save_moe | 96 | 2.867 s (137.2k tok/s) | 2.672 s (147.2k tok/s) |
235.7 GiB |

Step-19 loss agrees with the old kernels within 1e-4. Earlier batch-96
runs on these kernels took 4.5-5.0 s per step, and one ran out of
memory. Those runs reused XLA autotuning results from the per-fusion
autotune cache, which JAX keeps inside `--compilation-cache-dir`. With
that cache off (`JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`) or empty,
batch 96 runs at 2.66-2.70 s and its throughput is above batch 64. The
kernels were not the cause: per call they are 25-35% faster at batch
96's M=196608. With a warm autotune cache, save_moe at batch 64 took
4.95 s per step on the new kernels and 5.62 s on the old ones. With
fresh autotuning it took 1.83 s and 1.99 s. Jobs: 453914, 453961 and
453944 (A/B), 453791 and 453823 (cache reproduction).

The per-call numbers and the block-size sweep came from
`lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which is in
#9894. The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows
past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both
families on a GPU. The tile-map family also runs them on CPU through the
Pallas interpreter. Tests passed on MI350X (job 453882) and on the CPU
interpreter (job 453881), and again after rebasing onto current main:
all 72 on MI350X (job 458117), and on MI300X 42 passed with the 30 f32
cases skipped (job 458116). f32 cases skip on NVIDIA and on gfx942
(MI300X, MI325X), because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 there.
`test_accelerator_implementation_value_and_gradients_match_xla` now runs
at highest matmul precision, as #9922 did for the custom VJP test: at
default precision, XLA's autotuner on MI300X decides per process whether
f32 dots run in xf32, and the test failed in 3 of 5 MI300X runs. With
the change it passed 10 of 10 (job 458222).

Background and earlier measurements:
https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027367267

Part of #9812

Add structure closure checks to VerifyIt (#10093)

Expose structure-completion checks from VerifyIt: partial JSON and
delimiter classification, content-preserving scoring, and tool-call
markup diagnostics. The shared checks do not depend on RolloutEngine's
model calls or session lifecycle. SkyRL can use the published VerifyIt
package for grading while keeping token repair in its trainer.

Callers supply their generation stop markers. JSON value comparison uses
VerifyIt's existing strict-type comparator. The full VerifyIt suite
passes (1,469 passed, 2 skipped); the 89 focused closure and markup
cases pass, and Pyrefly reports zero errors. The built wheel includes
all three modules.

[Marin #10078](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10078) can
remove its RolloutEngine copies when it rebases. [SkyRL
#965](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/965) will
switch its closure imports and drop its duplicate markup parser after
this package is published.

Build ports worker images and serve durable catalogs (#10072)

Serve the durable guest ports publication prefix over HTTPS on
`cw-us-east-02a`. Cilium restricts ingress to Traefik and trusted Iris
clients and egress to DNS and the bucket endpoint. The proxy uses an
existing read-only object-store secret.

Pulumi builds one image from pinned Shellsim source, runs its proxy
command, and exports the same digest-qualified reference as
`workerImage`. The ports CLI reads that stack output by default and
accepts `--worker-image` for experiments. Image builds remain disabled
during preview.

When an older snapshot finishes after a newer release, log both versions
and preserve the stable catalog. Ports build and publication are
introduced in #10071; the shared image is in rjpower/shellsim#238.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch (#9689)

The scaling-ladder launcher holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update,
so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at
16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and
gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. The hero's context
length, QK multipliers, and capacity factor live in HERO_MODEL.
--qk-mult and --qk-mult-long-scale (global layers only) override the QK
multipliers for trial arms and ladder rungs; trial arms set the context
length on their branch alongside the history. Eval packs at the training
context, as on main, so the eval_dropless/* series shift at each switch.
For short trial arms, --eval-every overrides the eval cadence.

The hero's context history is checked in, like the data mix's switch
point: HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES in launch_scaling_ladder.py lists each
context the d6144 hero trained at before its current one with the step
it ended at, and HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL holds the parent's cumulative
training FLOPs at the last switch. A context-switch deploy PR edits
Python only: it sets the HERO_MODEL fields, appends one entry to
HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES, and sets HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL, so a second
switch (4K to 16K, then 16K to 64K) is described exactly and
trigger_hero.sh is unchanged. The launcher turns the history into a
FlopsBaseline at the last end step and, through the prior_context_phases
argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config, into
LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with each earlier phase's Harrier
stage schedule and shuffle blocks at its own batch size, so the Harrier
sources continue from their earlier reads. At d6144 the launcher rejects
a history that does not start at 4K, repeats a length between adjacent
phases (including the current context), or disagrees with whether the
baseline is set. LmDataConfig rejects end steps that do not increase,
and rejects any switch below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff
because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache. The
narrow rungs take no history.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh is identical to main and
launches the 4K HERO_MODEL with no FLOPs baseline. A switch still needs
a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds;
see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

Part of #9615

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Fail a length-cut structured reply without a repair (#10091)

complete_structured now raises StructuredOutputError as soon as a reply
ends with finish_reason length, carrying the completions so far, and
keeps the repair loop for every other validation failure.
A repair request replays the whole cut reply as the assistant turn, so
on a live run a reply cut at the 131k output limit made a repair prompt
of about 175k tokens, which overflowed the 262k context window with a
context_overflow 400.
The retry with max_tokens lowered to about 100k could not finish either,
since the repaired reply runs under the same output limit and the repair
only spends a full prompt.
The capability-driven task generator already catches
StructuredOutputError and records the failure on the item, so its
behavior is unchanged apart from the skipped repair request.

complete_structured now appends schema_instruction(output_type) as the
final user turn of every request and repair, a plain-text line per field
with its type and description, because the chat template renders nothing
from response_format and the model never saw the field names or
descriptions.
On a live run of 27 author calls, 16 needed a repair, and in every
sampled first reply the source field held a short label while the
program sat only in the reasoning, so each repair cost a second 40k to
100k-token reasoning pass and was the main path to the 131k output cut.

commits.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
commits.message:
Support agent-driven sessions in RolloutEngine (#10054)

Let callers register task sessions that prepare prompts, handle model
turns and tools, and grade an attempt. `RolloutEngine` owns model calls,
exact-token accounting, deadlines, and resource cleanup. The built-in
Shellbox session uses the same factory contract as registered sessions.

Each factory receives a `TaskSessionContext` containing the lowered
task, selected machine, and optional task grader. A session class with
`__init__(context)` registers directly; an adapter factory can bind
extra inputs for an external agent runner. `SessionGrader` tasks grade
themselves; sessions that delegate final grading call
`require_task_grader()`. `AgentTaskSession` adapts an agent's completion
callback to this contract. The engine records each model transport
message before passing it to a session, so a session can parse the
response and choose the next prompt without replacing the recorded
response. This change renames `ShellboxRolloutEngine` to `RolloutEngine`
and updates its callers in [SkyRL
#965](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/965).

TaskCompendium normalizes text-block chat content and retains non-object
tool arguments as transcript evidence; execution and final submission
still reject them. SkyRL's chat-template markup parser lives in
skyrl_gym, where its replay task and FTPO objective share it.

The RolloutEngine suite passes 111 tests, with 5 skipped and 3
deselected. The TaskCompendium suite previously passed 513 tests on this
branch. The current SkyRL #965 tree passes 757 gym tests and 357
targeted trainer tests with the pending APIs from this PR and
[#10078](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10078) overlaid
locally. Pyrefly reports zero errors and diff lint passes. The full
SkyRL trainer suite exceeded the local 8 GB memory limit during parallel
Ray tests.

After this and #10078 merge and the Python library family publishes,
SkyRL #965 can refresh its root and gym PyPI locks and rerun CI.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
Integrate portable ports into Shellbox rollouts (#10071)

Shellbox uses one `PackageSpec` for Python requirements and tools on both local bubblewrap and Shellsim machines. Bubblewrap resolves wheels once into a cached, read-only environment and requires tools in the sandbox PATH. Shellsim workers retain a Context that owns their catalog and cache policy. Task declarations pass the package selection unchanged to the chosen backend.

Agent shells persist across actions; verifier commands use fresh shell state over the same filesystem. Curation accepts a snapshot catalog URL.

Factories own execution-support checks for task semantics, capabilities, image origin and allocation features. Task lowering and preparation delegate to the selected factory. Docker and QEMU retain the requested machine spec while preparing their runtime inputs separately; QEMU bundle loading captures its declared image origin before support checks.

Native PackageSpec installation is wheel-only because environment preparation runs on the host. Existing explicit-lock installation retains source builds: the checked-in grader lock includes source-only `langdetect==1.0.9`.

Add the ports build/check/export CLI under `infra/shellsim`. Buildomatic owns BATCH execution and caching on `cw-us-east-02a`; shared assets and versioned catalogs publish to the durable CoreWeave prefix. Snapshots precede serialized stable promotion. Update the locked runtime to Shellsim 0.1.35.

The complete guest selection requires [Shellsim #235](https://github.com/rjpower/shellsim/pull/235).

commits.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
commits.message:
[inference] Start serve readiness timeout after placement (#10038)

Start the serve readiness timeout when a task's current attempt has an
assigned Iris worker or a node-bound Kubernetes pod, or when the task is
running. Kubernetes reports Kueue-gated Pending pods as BUILDING; the
previous state-count check treated them as placed and failed evaluations
after 2,400 seconds without allocating a GPU. Federated task status can
also show a peer display label as its worker ID before placement, so the
waiter uses the current attempt's assignment.

Queued time remains subject to the four-hour placement deadline.
Requeued attempts stop consuming the startup budget, and old attempts'
placement details do not mark the new attempt as placed.

Fixes #10036

[grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper (#9928)

The next PR in this stack, #9880, adds a `ring_dedup` expert-parallel
backend that selects each GPU's local expert assignments exactly the way
`ring` does. This PR moves that selection into a shared helper first, so
`ring_dedup` can call it instead of copying it.

`_select_local_assignments` in `ep_ring.py` covers the per-expert
counts, the prefix capacity cap, the top-k selection ordered by (local
expert id, flat position) and the padding of the `ragged_dot` group
sizes. The computation moves without edits, so ring's behavior is
unchanged. The existing ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py` pass on
8x MI350X (9 tests) and on CPU (6 tests; the 3 multi-device tests skip),
in job 455432.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds
for ROCm (base `main`). It also edits `ep_ring.py`, so this PR sits on
top of it.
2. #9928 this PR (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch)
3. #9880 [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE
backend (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, this PR's branch)

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for GPUs (#9860)

Add a `ring_gather_combine` MoE implementation: the ring expert-parallel
backend with its dispatch and combine done as gathers in both
directions. `implementation=None` resolves to it on GPUs, CUDA and ROCm
alike. On other backends, TPU included, `None` still resolves to `ring`,
which keeps the scatter-add combine, and `moe_implementation="ring"`
selects `ring` on any backend. Like the other expert-parallel
implementations, it runs only on an expert mesh axis of size two or
more. Without one, `moe_mlp` falls back to the local `scatter` path, so
a single-device call never reaches the gather code.

On AMD GPUs the combine `zeros_like(x_global).at[token_local].add(...)`
and the transpose of the dispatch `jnp.take` compile to scatter-adds
that run at about 0.8-1.2 TB/s. With `--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true`,
which RL training on H100 enables, XLA lowers GPU scatter-adds to sorts.
`ring_gather_combine` builds an inverse map from each (token, k)
assignment to the dispatch slot that holds it. The dispatch take and the
combine get custom VJPs, so activation rows move only by gather in both
directions: each token sums its at most K slot rows (K = 4 in the June
model). The inverse map itself is an int32 scatter-set
(`ep_common._assignment_sources`, 0.04 ms at June shapes), and the
routing-weight gradient still scatter-adds one scalar per slot, as in
`ring`. `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` takes the dispatch and combine pair as
an argument, and `moe_mlp` binds it when it picks the backend, so the
ring code has no platform check. The default is picked by
`resolve_moe_implementation` from `jax.default_backend()`, which
initializes JAX. The experiment configs' `__post_init__` checks can run
before `jax.distributed.initialize`, so they now call
`validate_moe_implementation`, which only checks the name. The combine's
profile scope is renamed from `scatter` to `combine`, the name the other
EP backends use.

In bf16 the two backends round differently. `ring_gather_combine` sums
each token's rows in f32 and rounds to bf16 once, in the combine and in
the dispatch gradient. `ring`'s bf16 scatter-add rounds after every add,
on CPU and on MI300X, so the two can differ in the last bits of a
token's sum. A bf16 test checks the gather sums bit for bit against an
f32 sum rounded once, on inputs whose products and f32 sums are exact.
On CPU the test fails if the sums run in bf16. On MI300X it cannot catch
that, because XLA on ROCm keeps the fused bf16 sum in f32. At June
shapes on one MI350X (job 453908), the combine matched an f32
scatter-add rounded to bf16 bit for bit. The order of a scatter-add's
f32 adds is unspecified, so other inputs can differ in the last bit.

With `implementation="ring"`, the traced program is the same as on the
merge base. Exporting its forward and backward for CUDA (8-way expert
parallelism, bf16) gives an identical jaxpr and debug-stripped StableHLO
with the XLA `ragged_dot`, and an identical jaxpr with the Triton
`ragged_dot` that H100 uses by default. Pallas Triton cannot be lowered
without a GPU, so that path was compared at the jaxpr level only. The
profile scope name is the only difference.

Step time with `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py`
and `--moe-impl` set to each backend: full June width and sequence
length (hidden 2560, 256 experts, top-4, seq 4096), cut to 4 layers to
fit 8x 80 GB, with 32,768 tokens per device and `recompute_all`. Each
figure is the median over steps 5-24 of two fresh-compile runs per
backend, alternating on one node (Iris jobs
`/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-b` and `/dev/ring-gather-9860-v5p8-b`):

| Hardware | XLA flags | `ring` | `ring_gather_combine` | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8x H100, EP8, `xla_flash` attention | default | 0.636 s | 0.623 s |
1.9% faster |
| 8x H100, EP8, `xla_flash` attention |
`--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true` | 3.232 s | 0.756 s | 4.3x faster |
| TPU v5p-8, EP4, `tpu_splash` attention | default | 1.064 s | 1.162 s |
9.2% slower |

Repeat runs agree within 0.4%. Losses agree within 2e-5 on H100 and are
identical on TPU.

The MI350X measurements below ran on an earlier revision that chose the
gather path with a ROCm check inside `ep_ring.py`. The gather code is
unchanged, except that the inverse map now comes from
`_assignment_sources`, which runs the same scatter-set.

Single-MI350X microbenchmark at June per-GPU shapes
(`bench_grug_ring_combine_top_k.py` from #9891, job 453908):

| | scatter-add | gather |
|---|---|---|
| combine forward | 2.420 ms | 0.969 ms |
| dispatch + combine, forward and backward | 5.436 ms | 1.790 ms |

Full June model, batch 64, flash attention, 8x MI350X, fresh compiles,
step time with the gather path and the routing top-k from #9889
together:

| remat policy | before | after | jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.823 s (12.40% MFU) | 1.735 s (13.03% MFU) | 453972 /
453979 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.848 s | 1.788 s | 453841 / 453957 |

Losses agree within 4e-4. These runs used the flash attention from #9853
and the tuned Triton `ragged_dot` from #9859. This PR does not depend on
either.

With the GPU default, `test_grugformer_moe.py` passes on CPU (job
461508) and on one MI350X, where the multi-device tests skip (job
461652). On 8x H100, `None` resolves to `ring_gather_combine` and every
ring test passes, including the one that hangs on MI300X. 6
`ragged_all_to_all` tests fail there, the same way on `main` (Iris jobs
`/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-tests` and
`/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-ragged-ab2`). The experiment-config tests
pass on CPU (job 461652). The ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py`,
including `ring_gather_combine` against `ring` with capacity drops, pass
on 8x MI300X (12 tests) and on CPU (9 tests; 3 in-process multi-device
tests skip) in job 456128. The bf16 test and the other
`ring_gather_combine` tests pass on 8x MI300X and on CPU in job 458228.
With #9928 and #9880 stacked on top, the 17 ring tests pass on 8x MI300X
in job 456022. Some MI300X runs hang in
`test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[all_valid-ring]`,
with one GPU busy and the other seven idle. The same test hangs on
`main` (job 456135: 2 of 4 runs on this branch, 1 of 4 on `main`). On 8x

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps (#8303)

Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the
store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three
co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf,
and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one
shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the
`QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it
unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage
bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw
scores,
and follows the data flow #9694 gave the reference quality step: one
Zephyr task
per shard on GPU workers reads each document's first 512 stored
`input_ids` from
the source's Nemotron tokenize leaf (`iter_tokenized_documents` regroups
chunk
rows) in lockstep with the normalized shard's ids, and the Harrier
embedding by
position. No tokenizer runs on the worker. The step depends on the
tokenize step
(`hero_data.tokenize_step_for(source, NEMOTRON_TOKENIZER)`), refuses a
tokenize
artifact built from another normalize output or tokenizer repository
before it
lists anything, and carries the tokenizer commit in its identity twice:
through
the tokenize dependency's hash and through the pin. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves
the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are
registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a
rerun of the score stage tokenizes the source again (the runner builds
the
dependency) and lands at the step's own identity. The content-type
leaves
written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen
step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in
its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized
order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs
by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard
(`AlignedColumn` for whole-column sides, `AlignedDocuments` for the
streamed
tokenize side), so a leaf from a different normalize run fails its
shard.
`QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is removed; the stage report reads
its
spot-check text from the normalized shard of the same basename, and the
reference
quality step from #9694 keeps its lockstep tokenize/normalize read
without the
samples side output.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`,
relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE,
frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta.
`load_pooled_scorer`
resolves the artifact stem from the directory, so the token-window
`PooledScorer`
from #9694 loads both `pooled_junkgate2_marin` and `nemotron_88k`.
`QualityPin`
carries separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration
file,
checked by the worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the
bucketed
dataset without moving or rescoring the raw scores. The calibration file
parses
into a `Calibration` dataclass (global or per-type curves);
`calibrate_model`
from #9694 writes it. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion
checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose
field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to
identical
weights and scores.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents
in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12
sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the
output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content
types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage was rerun on
`nsf_awards`
from the tokenize leaf (Iris job
`/muchanem/hero-quality-score-smoke-nsf`:
tokenize under Nemotron, then score against the pinned Harrier
embeddings) and
matched the pinned scores row for row, same ids and order, to a maximum
difference of 1.56e-3 (mean 2.28e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of
a
4,096-document batch against the earlier 32,768. A local end-to-end test
runs
`score_fusion` over hand-written tokenize and embedding leaves with a
tiny fusion
model and checks order, window truncation, chunk regrouping and the
refusals.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Add a separate QK multiplier for hero global layers (#10086)

Add `GrugModelConfig.qk_mult_long_scale`, an extra Q multiplier on the
hero's global layers (every `global_every`-th layer and the last: full
causal, RoPE disabled). Global layers multiply Q by `qk_mult` and then
by `qk_mult_long_scale`. Local sliding-window layers use `qk_mult`
alone. The field, its 1.0 default, and the order of the two multiplies
match `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/model.py` and the pinned vLLM
GrugMoE backend, which reads the same config key. A scale of 1.0 adds no
op, so the live hero and existing checkpoints trace unchanged. Otherwise
the layer scan's traced `is_global` flag selects the scale with
`jnp.where`, which keeps one scan body for all layers and covers both
RoPE paths.

Q and K are RMS-normalized, so the Q multiplier sets the softmax
temperature. Moving the hero from 4K to 16K context leaves the local
layers' 2048-token window unchanged, so the YaRN-style mscale, 1.3 ×
(0.1·ln(s) + 1), applies only to the global layers. Trial arms can raise
the global scale and hold the local layers at 1.3: a long scale of
1.1386 gives 1.48, and 1.2964 gives 1.68.

The HF config export writes `qk_mult_long_scale`. A config without the
key loads with 1.0. `launch_diagnostics.py` takes
`--qk-mult-long-scale`. `launch_scaling_ladder.py` and `trigger_hero.sh`
are unchanged because #9689 also changes them; the production flag will
follow after it lands.

Part of #9615

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch (#9890)

GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently
of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring
at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The dropless eval
reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative
throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline
(completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's
history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention
cost.

Stacked on #9888. Part of #9615

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Run the June synthetic benchmark across Slurm nodes (#10020)

`--gpus-per-node N` initializes jax.distributed from Slurm for one srun
process per node that owns local GPUs 0 to N-1, and `--replica-axis`
sets the Grug mesh's replica axis. Devices are ordered by process, so
the inner mesh axes stay within a node and the flags choose which axis
crosses nodes: on two 8-GPU nodes, `--expert-axis 8 --replica-axis 2`
gives data parallelism across nodes, `--expert-axis 8` alone gives FSDP,
and `--expert-axis 16` gives expert parallelism. Peak memory is now
reported for the process's local devices only. Every process uses rank
0's default run id, because per-process timestamps can differ and would
split one benchmark's logs and profiles across several ids.

The device ids are passed explicitly. Without them, JAX's Slurm
detection gives each process only the GPU numbered by its local rank,
and the AMD HPC Fund nodes set no CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for Levanter to
split.

On two MI350X nodes at 8 sequences per GPU, data parallelism across
nodes reaches 78% of one node's per-GPU throughput (2.023 s per step and
11.16% MFU, against 1.584 s and 14.26%). EP16 and FSDP across nodes
reach 70%. Those runs used an earlier form of the flag that read
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. On this branch, a two-node run of the medium
preset with `--gpus-per-node 8` builds the same 16-device mesh, and the
one-node default path is unchanged.

Part of #9812.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch (#9888)

Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed
2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are
identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer
context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the
same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle
window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would
have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining
~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context
lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With
prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the
shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next
window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips
about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes
per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give
positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops
zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a
change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same
sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could
continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the
source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked
from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come
from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also
absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at
16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new
LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

Part of #9615

commits.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
commits.message:
[iris] Retain terminal pods from their finish time (#10083)

Retain terminal Kubernetes pods from the latest init or regular
container `finishedAt`, including the output uploader. Ordinary pods
keep their one-hour window and gang pods keep their one-minute window.
GC previously measured both from pod creation, so an old task could lose
its pod immediately after completion or an init-container failure,
before reconciliation recorded its outcome.

Pods without a container finish timestamp continue to use creation time
for cleanup. GC-before-reconciliation regressions preserve success and
staging failure outcomes; 2,887 Iris tests pass on current `main`.

Fixes #10082

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Add the GLM client and a catalog task generator (#10068)

Add `lib/taskforge` with the GLM-5.3 client and an experiment that turns
capability catalog entries into TaskSpecs. For each capability, GLM
receives one prompt (the capability record, the TaskSpec JSON schema and
an example program) and replies with a program submission the server
constrains to that schema. The driver runs the program as a child
process in its own Python environment, in its own session, with only
`PATH` and a timeout, and keeps the output when it parses as a TaskSpec.
A model or program failure is recorded on its item; the run always
writes. The task carries its own verifyit grader; the driver checks
nothing else. All outputs (request, completions with usage and every
attempt, program, run record with the program's full stdout and stderr,
`task.json`) are written once, after every item finishes.

The client is the openai SDK over our own httpx client, with the SDK's
retries off so every request leaves an `Attempt` record. Around it sits
the policy the shared router needs: a retry budget with backoff, a hold
while the router reports an empty pool or no route, a per-token stall
timeout, continuation of replies cut by the output limit, and refusal of
a prompt that does not fit the context window (nothing is lowered or
truncated to make it fit; a continuation that overflows ends the call
with the output gathered so far). The endpoint comes from an
`EndpointSource` the client asks again whenever a hold starts, so a
relay that moves mid-run is picked up. Structured output is the server's
JSON-schema `response_format`, with client-side validation and one
repair turn for what the grammar cannot check. `LLMProviderConfig` holds
how the provider is called (model, attempts, hold, backoff, stall
timeout, connection pool, repair budget); `LLMPolicy` keeps only
sampling. The bearer token is read from the environment variable the
chosen pool selects (`GLM_BULK_TOKEN` or `GLM_HIGH_TOKEN`), as the other
post-training experiments do.

Taskforge runs as its own CI suite (`taskforge-unit`), with the client
tested against a local fake of the GLM router and the driver tested end
to end with a canned model. Run it live with the GLM router
port-forwarded to 127.0.0.1:18000:

```
GLM_HIGH_TOKEN=... uv run --package marin-taskforge --frozen python -m experiments.post_training.capability_driven_envs.generate_tasks --output-dir /tmp/capability-tasks --base-url http://127.0.0.1:18000/v1 --pool high
```

Draft #9993 holds the full pipeline design. Proposal, build, validation,
review and the stage coordinator follow as separate PRs cut from it.
